text: I appreciate that. We're really, I mean, this is, Norman Forward has been a game changer for public art in Norman. And we have been able to implement projects on a scale that has just exceeded a normal timeline for a public art program in a community. So this has been really great. So just to take everybody through this, kind of the history of how this all started. So on April 12th of 2016, the city of Norman contracted with the Norman Arts Council to administer the 1% of Norman Forward projects that were designated for art. When we worked with the city on this, we laid this out in kind of a very specific process. It's basically a four-step process for each project that has a percent of that project dedicated to art. We begin with project development in which we research projects of similar scale and purpose. And then we assemble a project team. That project team consists of a variety of people. It's representatives from the Norman Arts Council, representatives from the Public Arts Board, a representative from a stakeholder in the project. So that is usually somebody who is specifically related to that project. So whether that is staff at a facility where the project is being implemented or staff at the park where the project is being implemented, we always have an arts expert on our team. And that is somebody who is familiar with public art and can kind of serve as that guiding person on sort of the more technical aspects of is an art proposal applicable to the project? Can it be carried out and things like that? The city has a specific designee. And then we also always have a designee from the Norman Forward Project Ad Hoc Committee for that particular project. So once we kind of get through project development, we go into the selection process. Our selection panel is usually that project team. And that selection panel reviews are the submissions that we get in and the proposals. And ultimately they recommend the selected project, the selected art project to go along with the Norman Forward Project. After the art project is selected, which is kind of, it's sort of like that's the most public facing piece of the process. We then, we continue on with our involvement to execution and installation. And so we continue to coordinate between the city and the artist who was selected. We do this in the contracting process because the artist is actually contracting with the city of Norman. We facilitate the coordination of that. And then we also facilitate the coordination of checking in with the artist throughout the design process and organizing the facilitation of the installation itself with the people who are involved in the, whether it's the construction of the project or in a park, we facilitate that. And then we go on beyond that to public engagement and education. Public engagement is usually our sort of our ribbon cutting celebration of the art being installed. And then our education, we have developed a program called Public Art is Smart. And we wrap our public art projects into this program, which we use to engage Norman public school children in the public art in Norman. So that's kind of the overall process that we developed with the city of Norman. We have five projects to date, and I'm gonna go through each of these just to refresh your memories on this. The first project that we completed was Splash at the Westwood Swim Complex. This was installed and dedicated on December 7th, 2017. This was a $100,000 project, and it was awarded to a Florida artist, Mark Ayling. And this was his vision of a sculpture that is meant to be driven around and seen from 360 degrees as you navigate your way through the Westwood Complex. And we see a ball splashing into a splash of water. And the way that the sculpture itself is designed is that as you move around it, it almost has this visual movement to it as well. Our second project was Prairie Wind, and this was at the new Norman Public Library East. This project was installed and then dedicated on June 28th, 2018. This was a $32,000 project, and it was awarded to an Illinois artist, James Johnson. This project was really great. The artist responded not only to the architecture of the library, he responded to the site of the library, and it's a very interactive project that interacts with the summer solstice. And so on summer solstice, at a particular time of day, the light of the sun shines directly through the oculus in this sculpture and hits the building itself. The next project, and our largest to date, was Unbound at the Norman Public Library Central Branch, so the new library in Central Norman. We dedicated this on June 28th of 2018. This was a $260,000 project, and it was awarded to the London artist, Paul Coxedge Studios. This particular sculpture responds to the idea of all of the pages that are held within a library, and also the fleeting nature of printed pages, and referring to the idea that we transition into a more digital era, too. And so we see these pages being lifted up into the Oklahoma wind, into the sky, and this idea that pages are unbound. And that you can still visit the library, and you can hold, you can tangibly feel a book, but there are many other ways to experience a library as well. Our final completed project is Tryptic at Ruby Grant Park. We dedicated this just this past December. This was a $50,000 project, and it was awarded to Washington DC artist, Valerie Teberg. This project is meant to be a meditative, interactive project for visitors to Ruby Grant Park. Visitors are invited to sit, and touch, and feel, and look through Valerie's sculptural mosaic pieces. As they come to Ruby Grant Park, and walk through the trails, this piece is situated at a conjunction of the regular walking trails, and the cross-country trails within Ruby Grant Park. You can sit on the two smaller pieces, and see different points of view through the larger piece, which has, again, an oculus that looks completely through it, and you can see different perspectives of nature, and trees, and prairie lands, and the natural habitat of Ruby Grant Park. In the summertime, we haven't been able to visit this piece in the summertime yet, but we're really looking forward to that. This sits in a small glade, kind of on a little hill, and has a beautiful canopy of trees over it. So it'll be a really wonderful place to sit in the summertime, too, and just enjoy the park. And the project that we're currently working on that's in progress is at Andrews Park, and it's called In Their Words. Installation is scheduled for this coming summer. It's a $15,000 project, so one of our smaller budgeted projects, but I can assure you that there is a lot of this project to go through Andrews Park. This is by Oklahoma artist MJ Alexander. She's primarily known as a photographer in Oklahoma, but she has partnered with another artist to create this site-specific sculptural experience as you go through Andrews Park. This project is particularly, I think, interesting and poignant to Norman, Oklahoma, as Alexander's proposal was to integrate quotes from renowned Normanites over the course of our history as a community. And so quotes were selected by a special selection panel that included historians and the artist herself, and art experts, and park experts, experts, and these quotes were selected. They will be etched into the sidewalks throughout Andrews Park. These quotes will be etched in. And then in order to do that, the artist creates these large metal stencils in order to do this sort of etching into the sidewalks into a stencils type pattern. But we will reuse those stencils into a kind of sculpture garden in Andrews Park as well. So for this project, we will have both the etchings on the sidewalks itself and then a sculpture garden where the stencils will be displayed on stands and sunlight and shadow will shine through those and people will be able to experience these Normanite quotes in a second way within the park. And so we have been discussing and wanted to discuss with you and get some feedback on ideas of how to use these remaining funds. And of course, there are other potential projects that would be a good fit for these remaining funds. Of course, the Senior Center, which is part of Norman Forward, but was not one of the projects that was designated to have a percent for art assigned to it, is kind of a big one. The second is that we, within the Norman Arts Council, feel like establishing Ruby Grant as a sculpture park for future use would also be a good use of these remaining funds. And finally, we understand that Norman Regional and their Wellness Center on the Porter Campus has kind of become a part of this conversation and that they have committed funds to add to the Senior Center and that there's potentially maybe a partnership with Norman Regional to enhance the public art at the Senior Center as it goes into this Wellness Center at Norman Regional. And then I will just also add to that, that, of course, Anthony Francisco, who is obviously our finance manager with the City of Norman and also a Norman Arts Council board member who always advises us on these things, he recommends that we don't spend all of the $267,000 that we have remaining and that we hold some of those back. We've done a really great job of kind of staying under budget on these Norman Forward art projects, which is why we have this 267,000 leftover. And we still have four projects left. And if we add on a project or projects to this, that we wanna make sure that we have some funds set aside so that if a project happens to go over budget, that we have funds for that too. Another piece of this that I'll mention before we maybe start some discussion and some guidance for us is that when we designed this proposal for a 1% for art for these projects, we followed sort of national standards for 1% for art projects. And what that basically means is that a work of art that is part of a project, whether it's a facility or an infrastructure project, or redoing a park, adding a new park, that the art that is assigned to that project is commensurate with the scale of the project. So when we think about the senior center, for example, we think about what the size of the project would be, which is really why we included the Norman Regional Wellness Center on here too. So we understand that there's a certain amount of city funds going to the senior center, and there's a certain amount of funds from Norman Regional that are also going to the senior center. But if Norman Regional is adding another 10 million to that, well, that becomes $170,000 art project. And so it's important with a percent for art to keep your art project commensurate with the size of the overall project, with the scale of the project. speaker: erinngavaghan
text: Yeah, and thank you, Council Member Hall. This is a question that we get a lot in these types of projects. And the first thing that we always respond is that you kind of have to think of artists in the public art world from a higher level in that you think about Oklahoma artists and would you only want them to be eligible to apply for projects in Oklahoma? These are professional artists and you want them to have opportunities all over the world. And so when we do our art projects, we approach it with the same philosophy. Yes, we want Oklahoma artists to apply, but sometimes the best fit for the project is somebody who is not from Oklahoma. We do additional outreach to Oklahoma artists. I mean, they are the artists who see our request for qualifications go out. They're the ones who see it most readily. They have the most reminders and opportunities to apply for a project. We also host workshops specifically for Oklahoma artists and Norman artists to help them be more competitive in public art projects. So those are the kinds of things that we do to nurture our local artists. But the biggest thing is that you have to think about our local artists in that do you want them to be confined just to Oklahoma? And no, you don't, which is why these public art projects are open to artists from anywhere. You want our local Oklahoma artists like Paul Moore and Jonathan Hills, who are some of our more renowned public art artists in Oklahoma to have opportunities all over the world. So we take that same philosophy here when we're putting out our public art projects. The one exception so far in the Norman Forward projects has been the Andrews Park project. Because that project had a smaller budget and because of the management of a project and how you have to work with artists, because it was a smaller budget, we did limit that to just Oklahoma artists to apply to that project. Because that particular project really wasn't feasible for an artist from out of state or even out of the country to apply for because we require that artists who are finalists come and do a site visit. They have to come and see the site as a finalist before they make their final presentation. They need to understand the community and the space where the art installation is gonna take place. And then we also require them to come back a second time to make their final presentation with a design to that selection committee. And so for a smaller project of that size, that's not realistic to ask to get an artist from out of state or out of country to be able to facilitate a project on that budget. We would not get the quality of project that we're getting with a local artist on that budget. So for that one particular, we did limit it to just Oklahoma artists, but on these larger products, we do open it up because there is more opportunity for artists with their imaginations to come in from out of state places. But rest assured, we do give local artists more opportunity to respond and to interact with us as they're preparing their presentations than we do artists from out of state.
